company_stages.label: Solo-founder side project, free beta
company_stages.summary: The founder started Plausible alone in December 2018 as a simpler, privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative. He ran a free beta with no subscriptions for about five months. Sources disagree on the beta date: one says January 2019 on Indie Hackers, another says February.

company_stages.label: Solo, paid but low MRR
company_stages.summary: Paid subscriptions launched in May 2019 with 60 beta users, ending that month at $64 MRR. It took 324 days to reach $400 MRR. MRR was flat in January 2020 because of high churn, and about 25% of revenue went to transaction fees. Sources disagree on the customer count when the marketer joined: fewer than 100, about 100, or a couple hundred / a few hundred.

company_stages.label: Profitable small team scaling ARR
company_stages.summary: Plausible was a profitable two-person team in 2021 and declined VC approaches. It reached $500k ARR ($42,624 MRR) in October 2021 and $1M ARR on 2 June 2022 with 7,000+ subscribers. The team grew to four.

company_stages.label: Established independent, profitable company
company_stages.summary: Plausible remains self-funded and profitable, with a team of 8 to 10. Reported subscriber counts rose over time: 12,000+, then more than 15,000, then more than 21,000. It says it multiplied its $1M ARR several times in the following three years. It has turned down investment offers.

strategy_phases.label: Build in public and niche communities
strategy_phases.summary: The founder shared progress on a blog, Twitter and Indie Hackers. All early users came from these build-in-public updates. For about a year, blog posts, outreach and HN posts brought only minor success.

strategy_phases.label: Content marketing and positioning against Google Analytics
strategy_phases.summary: After a co-founder joined, Plausible repositioned itself as an explicit Google Analytics alternative. It published blog posts weekly or more often. Several posts reached the Hacker News front page, and Google search became the top source of trial signups.

strategy_phases.label: Open-source self-hosting and copyleft relicensing
strategy_phases.summary: Plausible released a Docker self-hosted beta in June 2020 and v1 in October 2020. In October 2020 it moved from MIT to AGPL to stop corporations reselling its code. Both announcements topped Hacker News.

strategy_phases.label: Capturing regulatory and incumbent-change demand
strategy_phases.summary: Plausible saw increased interest after the Austrian DPA ruling against Google Analytics. It shipped a Google Analytics import tool, and launched funnels and revenue goals timed to the Universal Analytics sunset.

strategy_phases.label: Open core and conversion refinement
strategy_phases.summary: Plausible kept premium features cloud-only, renamed the self-hosted release to Community Edition and introduced a Business plan. In 2026 it simplified its homepage to improve trial conversion.

tactics.name: Opinionated anti-incumbent essay seeded to developer communities
tactics.description: Write a long post arguing against the dominant tool and share it on Hacker News, Reddit, Lobsters, Indie Hackers, Twitter and Mastodon.
tactics.mechanism: It reaches audiences already skeptical of the incumbent, and front-page placement brings concentrated traffic and trials.

tactics.name: Position the homepage as 'the alternative to X'
tactics.description: Rewrite the homepage headline to name the incumbent and compare against it directly.
tactics.mechanism: Visitors immediately understand what the product replaces, which suits searchers already looking for an alternative.

tactics.name: Homepage simplification for trial conversion
tactics.description: Move the feature grid up, cut prose, sharpen CTA labels and use credible testimonials.
tactics.mechanism: Reduces friction for non-logged-in visitors arriving on the homepage.

tactics.name: Social listening for incumbent complaints
tactics.description: Monitor Twitter, HN and Reddit for people complaining about the incumbent and engage with them.
tactics.mechanism: Reaches pre-qualified people at the moment of frustration.

tactics.name: No-card free trial with live public demo
tactics.description: Offer a 30-day trial without a credit card and place a live demo dashboard at the top of the homepage.
tactics.mechanism: Lets prospects evaluate without registration or sales calls.

tactics.name: Open-source the code to make privacy claims verifiable
tactics.description: Publish the full codebase so privacy-sensitive buyers can inspect it.
tactics.mechanism: Builds trust in a privacy niche and leads people to write about and recommend the product.

tactics.name: Copyleft relicensing against resellers
tactics.description: Switch from a permissive license to AGPL while keeping the cloud and self-hosted offerings intact.
tactics.mechanism: Stops corporations from building proprietary resale offerings without contributing back. The company says this supports sustainability.

tactics.name: Migration tool timed to an incumbent's sunset
tactics.description: Build an importer from the incumbent ahead of a forced migration deadline.
tactics.mechanism: Lowers switching cost exactly when users have to move anyway.

tactics.name: Comparison and educational content for search
tactics.description: Publish 'vs.' pages against competitors and educational guides alongside feature releases.
tactics.mechanism: Captures search traffic from people evaluating alternatives.

tactics.name: Self-hunted Product Hunt launch without prep
tactics.description: Launch on Product Hunt without pre-announcing or soliciting upvotes; promote through your own channels and an in-app badge.
tactics.mechanism: Relies on existing customers and followers for upvotes.

outcomes.summary: The April 2020 anti-Google-Analytics post produced record traffic and signups: 62.8k visitors in April and 272 signups, plus 166 trials in its first week, more than the prior four months combined.
Plausible says repositioning its homepage as a Google Analytics alternative in April 2020 started its growth. MRR went from $400 in April 2020 to over $10,000 nine months later.
The switch to ClickHouse cut graph load time from 5–6s to about 500ms and let Plausible onboard larger sites. The company says this enabled its growth.
Plausible says the AGPL change helped it build a sustainable open source project.

Product Hunt delivered modest results, and sources report different figures: 1,000+ visitors and 15 trials; 1,490 visitors and 22 trials in the first 24 hours; 2,560 visitors and 36 trials after almost a week; 2.8k visitors and 50 signups. Plausible considers Product Hunt not a sustainable long-term channel.
March 2022 was the best month for net MRR growth ($8,247), coming after the Universal Analytics sunset announcement and the Austrian DPA ruling. The link is based on timing.

Donations were negligible compared with subscriptions: six $5 donations in about six months.

thirty_second.text: Plausible is an open source, cookie-free web analytics tool that a solo developer started in December 2018 and later ran with a marketing co-founder. It has never paid for ads, affiliates or sponsorships. Its growth has come mainly from opinionated blog posts that reached the Hacker News front page, comparison and educational content that ranks in Google, and word of mouth. Revenue comes only from subscriptions to the hosted version, priced by pageviews with a 30-day free trial. It reached $1M ARR in June 2022, and later reported more than 21,000 paying subscribers and over 29,000 GitHub stars.

origin.text: The founder began building Plausible around December 2018. While working on a startup, he was asked to install Google Analytics. He did not trust it, and he found existing alternatives such as Simple Analytics and Fathom too barebones. He set out to build a simpler Google Analytics alternative with better privacy, offering '80% of the benefit with 20% of the complexity'. He planned never to store IP addresses or sell data, and considered open-sourcing the code so people could verify those claims.

first_users.text: Before writing much code, the founder published a blog post describing the tool he wanted and recruited beta users through Twitter and email. About 20–30 people showed interest. The beta was announced on Twitter and Indie Hackers, not through a big launch; sources place it in January or February 2019. All early users came from these build-in-public updates, and early users were mostly developers and personal bloggers. Paid plans opened in May 2019 to about 60 beta users, who got a third off. That month ended at $64 MRR.

flywheel.text: The claims point to a loop in which content and open source feed each other. A co-founder's posts against Google Analytics, and his posts about open source, repeatedly reached the Hacker News front page. Those posts drove traffic and trials, and spilled over to GitHub, where Plausible appeared on the Trending list. Open source code and aligned values led people to write about and recommend Plausible. Educational and comparison posts built steady Google search traffic, which became the top source of trial signups. Paying customers then spread the word. Several GitHub star spikes happened around the same days as Plausible-related Hacker News posts, for example April 8, 2020, July 27, 2020, October 6–13, 2020 and March 7, 2021. That overlap is timing only.

did_differently.text: Several choices stand out. Plausible positioned itself directly as 'the alternative to Google Analytics', which the company says started its growth. It made cookie-free tracking the default, so customers do not need consent banners. It refused paid advertising, affiliate programs and sales calls, even when some publishers declined to list it for having no affiliate program. It published traffic and revenue numbers openly. It relicensed from MIT to AGPL in 2020 after larger companies sought to resell its self-hosted version, and later moved some premium features to the cloud-only offering. Whether these choices drove growth more than broader privacy trends is not settled; a co-founder also credits the general privacy trend.

key_takeaways.text: A single positioning change and one essay coincided with a sharp change in traction. After 324 days to reach $400 MRR, Plausible got 272 trial signups in April 2020, more than the previous nine months combined. The founder attributes this to the 'stop using Google Analytics' post and the repositioning that accompanied it.

Hacker News traffic came in spikes, while search was steadier and converted better. In August 2020, Google organic search had the highest trial conversion rate, at 3.52%. The company calls Google its top source of trials and treats Product Hunt as unsustainable for long-term acquisition.

Open source appears to have served as both a trust signal and a distribution channel in a privacy niche. Self-hosting releases and the license-change announcement drew Hacker News attention and GitHub visitors. However, donations from self-hosted users stayed small, at six $5 donations in about six months.

Plausible built product features around changes at the incumbent, such as a Google Analytics import tool and funnels timed to the Universal Analytics sunset. March 2022, the month Google announced the sunset, was Plausible's best month for net MRR growth up to then. Interest also rose after the Austrian DPA ruling against Google Analytics.

Conversion work still mattered late in the company's life. According to the company, a few days of homepage edits in January 2026 were followed by an 84% rise in trial signups from non-logged-in visitors by April 2026, while traffic rose about 2%. The company reports that April 2026 was its best month for new paying subscribers.
Bootstrapping meant slower early economics: the company says January 2021 was the first month revenue covered its costs, and it acknowledges slower growth than VC-backed rivals as a tradeoff.
